Quick buying tips

  • Measure twice. Room, doorways, hallways and stair turns — in that order. Use our sofa size finder if you're unsure.
  • Check the frame. Hardwood frames outlast softwood and engineered wood by years. It's the single biggest quality signal.
  • Sit test the seat depth. 55–60 cm suits most adults; deeper (65 cm+) is lounge territory but can be uncomfortable for shorter sitters.
  • Read the delivery terms. "Free delivery" sometimes means kerbside only. Room-of-choice delivery is worth paying for with heavy sofas.
  • Ask about the guarantee. One year is the minimum you should accept; three to five years signals a manufacturer that trusts its frame.

Sofa FAQs

What size sofa do I need for a small UK living room?

For a typical small UK living room (around 3.5 × 3 metres), a 2-seater sofa (140–170 cm wide) or a compact 3-seater (under 190 cm) works best. Leave at least 75 cm of walkway around the sofa so the room doesn't feel cramped.

Is fabric or leather better for a sofa in the UK?

Fabric is warmer, cheaper and comes in more colours, but stains more easily. Leather is hard-wearing and easy to wipe clean but costs more and can feel cold in winter. For homes with kids or pets, a tightly woven fabric or treated leather is the most practical choice.

How much should I spend on a sofa in the UK?

A decent 3-seater sofa in the UK costs £400–£800 in 2026. Budget options under £350 exist but often use weaker frames. Spending £800–£1,500 gets you better suspension, denser foam and longer guarantees.

Will a new sofa fit through my door?

Measure your narrowest doorway, hallway and staircase turn before ordering. Most UK internal doors are 76 cm wide. Many sofas come with removable legs or in two sections — check the product dimensions against your measurements, not just the room.

Do sofas come assembled in the UK?

Most UK sofas arrive in one or two pieces with only the legs or feet to attach — a ten-minute job. Corner sofas usually arrive in sections that clip together. White-glove delivery with packaging removal is often available for an extra £20–£50.

Quick buying tips

  • Match the mattress size exactly. UK sizes are standardised — single 90×190, double 135×190, king 150×200, super king 180×200 cm.
  • Inspect the slats. Sprung slats flex and suit most mattresses; solid slats need gaps under 7 cm to support foam mattresses properly.
  • Measure the room, not just the bed. Allow 60 cm each side for getting in and out, and check the headboard height against windowsills.
  • Storage beds need clearance. Ottoman beds need room to lift; drawer divans need 60 cm of pull-out space.
  • Spend on the mattress first. A £200 frame with a £500 mattress sleeps better than the reverse.

Bed FAQs

What are standard UK bed sizes?

UK bed sizes are: single 90×190 cm, small double 120×190 cm, double 135×190 cm, king 150×200 cm, super king 180×200 cm. Always buy the mattress in the same size as the frame.

Is an ottoman bed worth it?

If you're short on storage, yes. An ottoman bed gives you the entire under-bed area as storage — roughly four large suitcases' worth in a double. The gas-lift mechanism should feel smooth and stay open safely on its own.

Divan or bed frame — which is better?

Divans are practical: compact footprint, often with drawers, and easy to move. Bed frames (wooden or upholstered) look better and suit larger rooms. For small UK box rooms, a divan usually wins on practicality.

How much should a good bed cost in the UK?

A solid double bed frame costs £250–£600 in 2026; ottoman and TV beds run £500–£1,200. Below £200, check the slat quality and frame joints carefully — that's where cheap beds fail.

Do I need a new mattress with a new bed?

Not necessarily, but check the fit: UK mattresses and frames are standardised, so your old mattress fits if it's the same size. If your mattress is over 8 years old or sagging, replace both together for the best sleep.

Quick buying tips

  • Do the wobble test. In-store or on arrival: press opposite corners of the table. Any rock means poor joinery — send it back.
  • Sit for 10 minutes. Chair comfort reveals itself slowly. Shallow seats and hard backs become miserable by dessert.
  • Measure the chairs-out footprint. Tables are measured without chairs; add 75–90 cm all round for pushed-back chairs.
  • Check the extension mechanism. On extending tables, read buyer reviews specifically about the mechanism — it's the number one failure point.
  • Think about cleaning. Glass and marble-effect show everything; wood hides a multitude of sins.

Dining Set FAQs

What size dining table do I need?

Allow 60 cm of table width per person and 75–90 cm of pull-out space behind each chair. A 120 cm table seats four; a 180 cm table seats six. Measure your room before falling in love with a table.

Are extending dining tables worth it?

Yes if you host occasionally but live in a normal-sized home. A good extending table seats four daily and six to eight at Christmas. Check the mechanism in reviews — stiff or wobbly extensions are the most common complaint.

What is the most durable dining table material?

Solid wood (oak, acacia) is the most durable and can be refinished. Tempered glass looks light but shows every fingerprint. Marble-effect MDF looks premium for less but chips more easily than real stone.

How much does a good dining set cost in the UK?

A decent 4-seater dining set costs £250–£500 in 2026; 6-seaters run £400–£900. Extending and marble-effect sets sit at the higher end. Below £200, check chair joints and table stability carefully.

Do dining chairs come assembled?

Usually not — most UK dining chairs need 10–20 minutes of assembly each, typically just legs and a few bolts. Tables often come with the top and legs separate. It's straightforward work for one person.

Quick buying tips

  • Match your sleep position. Side sleepers need medium/medium-soft for shoulder and hip relief; back sleepers need medium-firm; front sleepers need firm.
  • Use the sleep trial. Your body needs 3–4 weeks to adjust. A 100-night trial is only useful if you actually commit to the adjustment period.
  • Protect it from day one. A £30 waterproof protector guards a £500 mattress — and most guarantees are voided by stains.
  • Check the base. Foam mattresses need solid or closely-spaced slats (gaps under 7 cm); sprung mattresses are more forgiving.
  • Measure your stairs. A king-size mattress doesn't bend around tight Victorian staircases — consider a mattress-in-a-box.

Mattress FAQs

What type of mattress is best for back pain?

A medium-firm mattress usually suits back pain best — firm enough to support the spine's natural curve, with enough give at the shoulders and hips. Orthopaedic (extra-firm) mattresses help some back sleepers but can cause pressure points for side sleepers.

Memory foam or pocket sprung — which is better?

Memory foam moulds to your body and isolates movement (good for couples) but can sleep warm. Pocket sprung mattresses breathe better and feel more traditional, with each spring responding independently. Hybrids combine both. Hot sleepers should lean sprung or hybrid.

How often should you replace a mattress in the UK?

Every 7–8 years is the standard guidance. Replace sooner if you wake with aches, the mattress visibly sags, or you sleep better in other beds. A mattress protector can add a year or two of life.

What mattress size do I need for a UK double bed?

A UK double mattress is 135 × 190 cm; a king is 150 × 200 cm; a single is 90 × 190 cm. Buy the mattress in exactly the same size as your bed frame — a 2 cm gap each side is normal, more than that means the wrong size.

Do mattresses in a box work as well as traditional ones?

Yes — vacuum-packed mattresses expand to full size within 24–72 hours and perform like traditional ones. They're far easier to get upstairs in UK homes with narrow staircases. Unwrap within a few weeks of delivery for best expansion.

How to Choose a Sofa: UK Buying Guide (2026)

The complete walkthrough — measuring, sizes, fabrics, frames, delivery and care.

In short: measure your room, doorways and stair turns first; choose a hardwood frame with pocket-sprung or high-resilience foam seats; pick fabric for warmth and value or leather for durability; and budget £450–£800 for a 3-seater that lasts. The five sections below walk you through each decision.

How do I measure for a sofa?

Measuring is the step everyone skips and the one that causes most returns. Do it in this order:

  1. The room: measure wall to wall where the sofa will sit. Note radiators, plug sockets and door swings that eat into the space.
  2. The walkways: you need at least 75 cm of clear passage around the sofa — 90 cm is comfortable.
  3. The route in: measure your narrowest doorway (most UK internal doors are 76 cm), hallway width, and any staircase turns. Compare against the sofa's packaged dimensions, not just the sofa itself.
  4. The ceiling: for high-back sofas, check the height against windowsills and dado rails.

Standard UK sofa sizes (widths)

  • Loveseat / 2-seater: 120–170 cm — box rooms, snugs, flats
  • 3-seater: 180–220 cm — the average UK living room
  • Corner sofa: 230–300 cm — open-plan and large rooms
  • Seat depth: 55–60 cm suits most adults; 65 cm+ is lounge territory
  • Seat height: 43–48 cm is standard; higher suits taller or older sitters

Not sure what fits? Our free sofa size finder tool takes your room dimensions and recommends a size.

Fabric or leather — which should I choose?

There's no universal winner; it depends on your household. Here's the honest comparison:

FabricLeather
Price£300–£900 for a 3-seater£800–£2,000+ for a 3-seater
DurabilityGood; tightly woven lasts 7–10 yearsExcellent; 15+ years with care
CleaningStains need prompt treatmentWipes clean easily
ComfortWarm in winter, breathableCan feel cold initially, warm in summer
Kids & petsChoose stain-resistant weave; avoid light coloursTreated leather resists claws better than fabric
LookHuge colour/pattern choiceClassic, ages with patina

Our take: for most UK families, a mid-range fabric sofa with stain protection is the sweet spot — warm, affordable and replaceable. Leather earns its premium in homes where durability matters most (pets, teenagers, heavy daily use). Avoid "bonded leather" — it's plastic-coated scraps that peel within a few years.

What makes a good sofa frame?

The frame is the skeleton everything else hangs on, and it's where cheap sofas cut corners:

  • Hardwood frames (beech, ash, oak) are the gold standard — strong, stable, long-lived.
  • Softwood frames (pine) are fine at budget prices but can warp over time.
  • Chipboard / MDF frames are a red flag — they crack under stress and can't be repaired.
  • Joints should be screwed, glued and dowelled — never just stapled.
  • Seat suspension: pocket springs are best, followed by high-resilience foam (density 30 kg/m³+), then serpentine springs. Pure low-density foam sags within 2 years.

The showroom test: lift one front corner of the sofa about 15 cm. A good frame stays rigid; a poor one twists and creaks.

What should I know about sofa delivery in the UK?

UK sofa delivery: the facts

  • Timeframes: 2–4 weeks for stocked items; 8–12 weeks for made-to-order. Always get the estimate in writing.
  • Kerbside vs room-of-choice: "free delivery" often means kerbside only. Room-of-choice typically costs £20–£50 and is worth it for heavy sofas.
  • Packaging removal: usually £10–£30 extra — worth it, as sofa packaging is enormous.
  • Old sofa removal: many retailers offer it for £30–£60; councils also run bulky-waste collections.
  • Check access first: delivery drivers will refuse if it clearly won't fit — and you may still be charged.

How do I look after a sofa?

  • Plump and rotate loose cushions weekly — it evens out wear dramatically.
  • Vacuum fabric sofas monthly with an upholstery attachment (dust is abrasive).
  • Keep out of direct sun — both fabric and leather fade; rotate the sofa if one side faces a window.
  • Condition leather every 6–12 months to stop it drying and cracking.
  • Deal with spills immediately — blot, never rub. Keep a fabric cleaner matched to your upholstery type.

Sofa buying FAQs

What is the best sofa size for a UK living room?

For an average UK living room (4 × 3.5 m), a 3-seater of 190–210 cm works well. Smaller rooms suit 2-seaters (140–170 cm); large open-plan spaces can take corner sofas of 240 cm+. Always leave 75 cm of walkway around the sofa.

How do I know if a sofa is good quality?

Check three things: a hardwood frame (not just softwood or chipboard), pocket-sprung or high-resilience foam seats, and a guarantee of at least 2 years. Lift one corner — a quality sofa feels solid and doesn't twist.

Should I buy a fabric or leather sofa?

Fabric is warmer, cheaper and offers more colours; leather is harder-wearing and easier to clean but pricier. With kids or pets, choose a tightly woven fabric with stain protection, or a treated semi-aniline leather.

How long should a sofa last?

A well-made sofa lasts 7–15 years. Budget sofas (£250–£400) typically last 3–5 years before the frame or cushions give out. Rotating and plumping cushions regularly adds years of life.

What should I check about sofa delivery?

Confirm whether delivery is kerbside or room-of-choice, check the delivery timeframe (2–12 weeks is normal in the UK), measure every doorway and stair turn against the sofa's packaged dimensions, and ask about packaging removal.

How to Choose a Bed: UK Buying Guide (2026)

Sizes in centimetres, storage options, frames and mattress pairing — the full walkthrough.

In short: pick your size from the UK standard chart below (double 135×190 cm, king 150×200 cm), choose divan for small rooms or a frame for style, check slat quality before anything else, and budget more for the mattress than the frame. Details for each decision follow.

What are the standard UK bed sizes?

UK bed and mattress sizes are standardised — memorise this table and you'll never buy the wrong bedding again:

UK bed sizes (mattress dimensions)

SizeWidth × LengthBest for
Single90 × 190 cmKids, teenagers, guest rooms
Small double120 × 190 cmSingle sleepers wanting space; tight rooms
Double135 × 190 cmCouples in average UK bedrooms
King150 × 200 cmCouples wanting real elbow room
Super king180 × 200 cmLarge rooms; co-sleeping families
Emperor200 × 200 cmVery large rooms (bedding harder to find)

Key rule: the mattress must match the frame size exactly. European (e.g. 140×200, 160×200 cm) and US sizes differ — a "queen" is not a UK king.

Divan or bed frame — which is better?

DivanBed frame
FootprintCompact — same size as mattressLarger — headboard/footboard add 15–30 cm
StorageOften built-in drawersUsually none (unless ottoman)
LooksPlain and functionalWide style choice
MovingLight, splits in twoHeavier, bulkier
Price (double)£250–£500£250–£800+

Our take: for box rooms, rentals and kids' rooms, a divan is the practical winner. For main bedrooms where the bed is a design feature, choose a frame you love looking at.

What storage options are worth it?

  • Ottoman (gas-lift): the whole under-bed area becomes storage — about 4 large suitcases in a double. Best storage per pound. Needs clearance to lift.
  • Drawer divan: 2–4 drawers, easy daily access. Needs ~60 cm pull-out space beside the bed.
  • End-lift ottoman: lifts from the foot end — good when bedside tables block the sides.
  • TV beds: combine ottoman storage with a rising TV. A luxury, but the mechanism warranties (5 years on good ones) are reassuring.

Storage capacity guide (double bed)

  • Ottoman: ~800 litres — duvets, suitcases, out-of-season clothes
  • 4-drawer divan: ~300 litres — bedding, shoes, everyday items
  • 2-drawer divan: ~150 litres — sheets, spare pillows

How do I judge bed quality?

  • Slats first: sprung beech slats are best; solid slats need gaps under 7 cm (critical for foam mattresses). Fewer than 12 slats on a double is a warning sign.
  • Joints: look for bolted or bracketed joints — wobble the display model side to side.
  • Centre rail: doubles and above need a centre support rail with legs to the floor, or the middle sags.
  • Weight rating: check the maximum user weight — quality doubles handle 200 kg+ total.
  • Upholstery: on upholstered beds, press the padding — it should spring back, not stay dented.

Which mattress pairs with which base?

Mattress typeBest baseAvoid
Memory foamSolid platform or slats with <7 cm gapsWidely spaced slats (foam sags through)
Pocket sprungSprung slats (adds comfort)Nothing major — very forgiving
HybridSolid or close slatsWidely spaced slats
LatexSolid platform or close slatsSprung slats (too much flex)

See our best mattresses guide for specific picks.

Bed buying FAQs

What size bed do I need?

Choose by room and sleeper: single (90×190 cm) for kids and guests; double (135×190 cm) for couples in average rooms; king (150×200 cm) for comfort; super king (180×200 cm) for large rooms. Each person ideally gets 70–90 cm of width.

Are ottoman beds reliable?

Yes, if the mechanism is good. Look for gas-lift pistons rated for the mattress weight, a base that stays open on its own, and safety certification. Cheap ottomans with weak lifts are frustrating and can be unsafe — spend £500+ for a reliable one.

Do I need a headboard?

Not structurally, but headboards protect walls, make reading in bed comfortable, and finish the room. Many divans include one; most bed frames offer them as add-ons (£50–£150). Wall-mounted panels are a stylish alternative.

What mattress goes with which bed base?

Memory foam needs a solid or closely-slated base (gaps under 7 cm). Pocket sprung suits sprung slats. Platform tops suit everything. The mattress and frame must be the same UK size — e.g. a 135×190 cm mattress on a double frame.

How much should I budget for a bed and mattress?

For a double: £250–£600 for a good frame plus £250–£500 for a good mattress — £500–£1,100 all in. Spend proportionally more on the mattress; it affects your sleep far more than the frame.

Sofa Size Finder

Free tool · No signup · Instant answer. Enter your room dimensions and we'll recommend the right sofa size — with space left for doors, radiators and real life.

In short: measure your room's length and width, tell us the layout, and this tool calculates the maximum sofa width that still leaves a comfortable 75–90 cm walkway — then recommends a 2-seater, 3-seater or corner sofa to match.

How the recommendation works

  • Wall space: the sofa should span no more than two-thirds of its wall, leaving room for side tables and lamps.
  • Walkways: we reserve 75–90 cm of clear passage in front of and around the sofa.
  • Depth allowance: we assume a typical sofa depth of 90 cm when checking the room's other dimension.

Tool FAQs

How much space should I leave around a sofa?

Leave at least 75 cm of clear walkway around the sofa (90 cm is comfortable), and allow for door swings, radiators and other furniture. This tool factors walkway space into its recommendation automatically.

What is the standard depth of a sofa?

Most UK sofas are 85–100 cm deep. Compact 2-seaters can be 75–85 cm deep; deep lounge sofas and recliners reach 100–110 cm. Always check the product's depth, not just its width.

Will the recommended sofa fit through my door?

This tool recommends a sofa width for your room, but you must separately measure your narrowest doorway (usually 76 cm in UK homes), hallways and stair turns against the sofa's packaged dimensions before ordering.

About UK Furniture Guide

In short: UK Furniture Guide is an independent guide site helping British households buy furniture with confidence. We research products sold in the UK, publish honest pros and cons with real £ prices, and fund the site through affiliate commissions — which never influence our rankings.

Why we started

Buying furniture in the UK is harder than it should be. Product descriptions are written by marketing teams, "reviews" on retailer sites are cherry-picked, and American advice about sizes and delivery doesn't apply here. We started UK Furniture Guide to fix that: one site with practical, Britain-specific guidance — UK bed sizes in centimetres, realistic delivery timeframes, prices in pounds, and honest assessments of what survives kids, pets and daily life.

How we research

  • Specifications first: frame materials, construction methods, dimensions and guarantees — the things that determine how long furniture lasts.
  • Verified buyer feedback: we read hundreds of UK customer reviews looking for patterns, not outliers.
  • Price tracking: prices shown are checked against current UK retail and updated regularly.
  • Practical testing where possible: the showroom tests anyone can do — the wobble test, the corner-lift test, the sit test.

How we make money (honestly)

UK Furniture Guide is free to read and always will be. We make money when readers buy products through links on our pages — the retailer pays us a small commission at no extra cost to you. This is called affiliate marketing, and it's our only revenue stream alongside display advertising in the future.

Our promise: commissions never buy a ranking. Products are chosen on merit; if a product is poor value, we say so or leave it out — even if it pays the highest commission. Read the full affiliate disclosure.

Our editorial standards

  • No paid placements in rankings — ever.
  • Pros and cons on every recommendation, including the flaws.
  • UK-specific advice: sizes, prices, delivery and consumer rights.
  • Corrections published promptly when we're wrong — tell us.

Privacy Policy

Last updated: 4 October 2026

UK Furniture Guide ("we", "us") respects your privacy. This policy explains what information we collect when you use our website, why we collect it, and your rights under UK data protection law (UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018).

Information we collect

  • Information you provide: your name and email address if you contact us or sign up for our newsletter.
  • Automatically collected information: pages visited, time spent, device and browser type, and approximate location — collected via privacy-respecting analytics to help us improve the site.
  • Cookies: small files stored on your device. See below.

We do not collect sensitive personal data, and we never sell your personal information.

Cookies

We use a small number of cookies:

  • Strictly necessary cookies — required for the site to function (e.g. remembering cookie consent). No consent needed.
  • Analytics cookies — help us understand which guides are useful. Only set with your consent.
  • Advertising cookies — set by our advertising partners (e.g. Google AdSense, when enabled) to show relevant ads and measure performance. Only set with your consent.

You can withdraw consent or change your preferences at any time via your browser settings.

Affiliate links

Some links on this site are affiliate links. When you click one, the retailer may set a cookie to track the referral so we can earn a commission. This is covered in our affiliate disclosure. We do not receive your payment details or order information from retailers.

How we use your information

  • To respond to your messages and enquiries.
  • To send our newsletter, if you subscribe (you can unsubscribe at any time).
  • To improve our guides and tools through aggregated analytics.

Our lawful bases are consent (newsletter, non-essential cookies), contract (responding to enquiries) and legitimate interests (site improvement).

Data retention

Enquiry emails are kept for up to 24 months. Newsletter data is kept until you unsubscribe. Analytics data is aggregated and retained for up to 26 months.

Your rights

Under UK GDPR you have the right to access, correct, erase, restrict or port your personal data, and to object to processing. To exercise any right, email info@ukfurnitureonline.co.uk. You also have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) at ico.org.uk.

Changes to this policy

Home › Affiliate Disclosure

Affiliate Disclosure

Last updated: 4 October 2026 · Plain-English version of how this site makes money.

In short: UK Furniture Guide is reader-supported. When you buy through links on our pages, the retailer pays us a commission at no extra cost to you. Commissions never influence which products we recommend or how we rank them.

What is an affiliate link?

An affiliate link is a normal product link with a tracking code. If you click it and buy something, the retailer knows the sale came from us and pays us a percentage — typically 3–8% for furniture. The price you pay is exactly the same as if you'd gone to the retailer directly.

Which programmes do we use?

We participate in affiliate programmes including Amazon UK Associates and retailer programmes via networks such as Awin. The specific programmes are listed here as they're added: Amazon UK, Awin merchants (including Wayfair UK).

Does this affect our recommendations?

No — and this is the whole point of the site. Our editorial rules:

  • Products are researched and ranked on merit: quality, value, and suitability for UK homes.
  • Commission rates are never a ranking factor. A product that pays more but offers less will rank lower — or not appear at all.
  • Every recommendation lists honest cons alongside the pros.
  • We link to non-affiliate retailers too (for example, UK Furniture Online) where relevant, simply because it's useful.

What about display advertising?

In future we may show display advertisements (for example via Google AdSense). Advertisers don't influence our content either — editorial and advertising are kept strictly separate.

Why disclose this?

Because it's the law (UK consumer protection rules require clear disclosure of commercial relationships) and because it's the right thing to do. Trust is the only asset a guide site has — we'd rather over-explain than leave you guessing.

Questions? Contact us or read about our editorial standards.
